checkpoints: 'Correct by design' only proves the ledger is consistent with itself — it says nothing about whether it matches the outside world

Real systems drift for reasons the code can't see: clock skew, an on-call editing SQL by hand to unblock a customer, a deploy that patches only new transfers, a bank fee or correction landing after settlement, or a lost response causing a client to retry and apply twice
Reconciliation is an external immune layer that compares the ledger against an independent authoritative source — a bank statement, a processor settlement file, a partner drop
Because that source is independent of your code, it catches exactly the drift the code cannot detect
When the ledger and the external source disagree, the external source wins and the ledger converges via a compensating entry
Internal invariants and reconciliation are complementary layers, not substitutes
Idempotency is really a question of where the dedupe state lives and at what scope, and both proposals put it in the wrong place
An in-memory Set is per-process and non-durable — a restart wipes it, and every replica keeps its own copy, so a retry landing on a different instance sails through as if it were new

Moving the set into Redis fixes durability and sharing across replicas, but does not fix the race: two workers can both read 'txnId not seen' at the same instant and both proceed to insert — check-then-act is not atomic just because the check moved to a shared store, and neither an in-memory Set nor a Redis lookup can ever be a real guarantee, since both are a separate read-then-decide step a concurrent request can slip between before either has written anything
The only correct primitive is the database unique constraint on (txnId, accountId, direction) on ledger_entry, because the uniqueness check is atomic with the insert itself
On a race, exactly one INSERT commits and the other raises a unique violation (Postgres 23505) that the service catches and turns into a 'replayed' response

An app-level or Redis check is fine as a fast path to skip an obviously-duplicate request before it reaches the database, but the unique constraint is what makes the design correct under any concurrency or retry storm

Taking row locks in the order arguments happen to arrive in a request — first `fromAccountId`, then `toAccountId` — instead of a deterministic order makes the lock acquisition sequence depend on transfer direction, which is the actual root cause of an intermittent Postgres `deadlock detected` error, not anything wrong with the SQL itself.

When a transfer A→B and a concurrent transfer B→A both run `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on the same two accounts in opposite orders, the A→B transaction locks A and then blocks waiting for B, while the B→A transaction locks B and then blocks waiting for A — each transaction ends up holding exactly the row the other one needs next, forming a classic ABBA cycle.

Postgres's deadlock detector recognizes this wait-for cycle and resolves it by aborting one of the two transactions with a `deadlock detected` error while letting the other proceed, which is why the failure surfaces as an intermittent 500 rather than a hang.

Single-direction transfers on a given account pair never trigger this deadlock because only one transaction is touching the pair at a time — the cycle only forms when two transactions traveling in opposite directions race on the same pair of accounts concurrently.

The fix is to make lock acquisition order independent of transfer direction by sorting the two account ids and always locking the smaller one first, ideally in a single query such as `SELECT ... FROM account WHERE id = ANY($1) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` with the id array pre-sorted.

Once both A→B and B→A requests are forced to acquire the same first row regardless of which way the transfer is going, the second transaction simply queues and waits behind the first instead of each grabbing a different row and forming a cycle, so the deadlock cannot occur.
Transfers between disjoint account pairs never contend on the same row, so imposing a deterministic lock order costs nothing in throughput — full parallelism is preserved for unrelated transfers.

The fix should be verified by firing many concurrent A→B and B→A transfers on the same account pair under load and confirming zero `deadlock detected` errors, correct final balances on both accounts, and an intact `SUM(DEBIT) = SUM(CREDIT)` invariant across the ledger.

In a saga orchestrator, writing the `saga_step` audit row only after the HTTP call to the downstream service returns — on both the success and failure branches — means no row exists at all for the entire duration of that call.

The blind window sits between the moment the downstream service (wallet-service) applies its side effect (the debit) and the moment `sagaSteps.save(...)` actually executes; a crash inside that window leaves zero trace that the step was ever attempted.

Because there is no row until after the call resolves, a recovery scan cannot distinguish a step that never ran from one that ran and never got a chance to record its result — both look identical: absence of a row.

That ambiguity leaves the recovery process with no basis to decide whether to resume the step or run a compensating transaction, so a real debit can end up applied against the wallet with nothing in the durable log to account for it.

The correct ordering is write-ahead: persist a `saga_step` row with status `started` before the HTTP call to wallet-service is made, then update that same row to `ok` or `failed` once the response (or error) comes back.

Write-ahead ordering makes the durable `saga_step` table, rather than the in-memory stack frame of the `call()` function, the actual source of truth for what the orchestrator was doing when it crashed.
A `started` row with no subsequent `ok`/`failed` update is not leftover noise — it is precisely the marker a recovery scan looks for to identify an in-doubt step that needs follow-up.

Once an in-doubt `started` row is found, the orchestrator can query wallet-service using the `sagaId` plus step identifier as an idempotency key to determine whether the debit actually applied, and only then decide to resume the saga or trigger compensation.

Balances stored in minor units (cents, VND, satoshi) routinely exceed `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1) once an account grows large enough, and JavaScript's `Number` type cannot represent integers beyond that boundary exactly.

Coercing a minor-unit string balance through `Number(...)` before subtracting, as in `Number(truthBalance) - Number(ledgerBalance)`, rounds to the nearest representable double once the value crosses that boundary, producing a computed drift that is off by whole units of currency with no error or warning.

The reconciliation endpoint returns `drift` as a JSON number rather than a string, so even a correctly computed backend value gets re-coerced into floating point a second time by any client that deserializes that field, doubling the exposure to precision loss.

The write path carries an identical defect: `parseAmount` calls `parseFloat(raw)` on a transfer amount, so a large transfer can be rounded before it ever reaches the ledger, corrupting the very entries the reconciliation job is meant to check.

This class of bug is more dangerous than a typical crash because it is completely silent — nothing throws, no assertion fails, and the system just writes a compensating entry with a slightly wrong amount, so the double-entry invariant can drift for weeks before anyone notices.

The fix is to perform every arithmetic step on money — parsing, subtraction, and any derived compensating amount — using `BigInt` instead of `Number`, and to parse with `BigInt(raw)` so that malformed input like `"12.5"` throws instead of being silently truncated.

Every money field must be serialized back out as a JSON string rather than a JSON number, since no numeric JSON representation can survive re-coercion by a downstream consumer without risking the same precision loss.

Correctness should be verified by seeding a drift value above 2^53, asserting that the computed drift and compensating amount are exact to the unit, and asserting that the response body carries those amounts as strings rather than numbers.
replicas: N is not an imperative 'create N Pods and done' command — it is a declaration of desired state: 'I want N Pods to always exist'

A controller (the ReplicaSet the Deployment spawns) runs a continuous reconcile loop: it reads the actual state, compares it to the desired N, and acts to close the gap — creating more if short, deleting extras if over

Deleting a Pod by hand drops the actual count to N-1; on the next reconcile pass the controller detects the gap and creates a replacement, which carries a different name because it is an entirely new object, not the old Pod coming back to life

This is called self-healing rather than 'a script re-ran' because nobody wrote an explicit if-Pod-dies-recreate branch — the behavior emerges naturally from continuously comparing actual against desired
That same reconcile mechanism is why scaling is just editing the number N and letting the controller handle the rest — not a separate feature, the identical loop under a different name

Declarative beats imperative here because you never have to write logic for every possible way a Pod could disappear (node failure, OOM, manual delete, rolling update) — you declare the target state once and the controller keeps it true forever

The precondition for this to work at all is that the Deployment's selector.matchLabels must match the Pod's template.metadata.labels exactly — the only thread the Deployment uses to recognize 'which Pods are mine'
Get the label wrong and the Deployment manages no Pods, making the reconcile loop effectively inert
A cloud LoadBalancer is L4 — it only forwards TCP/UDP packets and hands out exactly one public external IP, with no idea which host or path an HTTP request is calling
Each LoadBalancer costs money every month, so letting every Service request its own wastes public IPs and burns unnecessary cost
The standard shape is only ONE cloud LoadBalancer (L4) pointing at the NGINX Ingress Controller, the only thing sitting behind that LoadBalancer
The Ingress Controller at L7 reads each request's host/path and fans out to many internal ClusterIP Services, so adding a new service only needs one more Ingress rule, not a new LoadBalancer
Ingress is the single place TLS termination happens: HTTPS is decrypted once at the edge, where the Ingress Controller holds the TLS secret cert-manager automatically writes into
After that, only plain HTTP flows onward to the ClusterIP Service inside the cluster's private network, so certificates are managed and renewed from one spot instead of scattered across every Service
The trade-off is an extra L7 hop and one more component (the Ingress Controller) to operate, in exchange for saving public IPs/cost and consolidating edge logic in a single place
Exposing the backend directly via Service `type: LoadBalancer` is wrong for production on two axes: cost/scaling and security.

Cost/scaling: each such Service makes the cloud auto-provision one dedicated LoadBalancer plus one public IP, billed separately every month, with no host/path routing between services — this doesn't scale: N services exposed this way means N LoadBalancers billed N times, plus N separate public IPs to manage.
Security: there is no `tls` block, so there is no TLS termination at all — traffic on the raw external IP is plain HTTP, unencrypted and readable by anyone in the middle.
The production-standard shape: the backend goes back to being a ClusterIP Service, with no dedicated public IP and not exposed straight to the Internet.
Put exactly ONE LoadBalancer in front of an NGINX Ingress Controller.
The Ingress routes by host/path down to the Services behind it.
TLS is terminated right at the Ingress using a certificate cert-manager auto-requests from Let's Encrypt via ACME.
This bare exposure is an acceptable shortcut for a quick internal dev/test setup, but it is a genuine blocker once shipped to production.

Every `GET /items` call falls straight through to MySQL even though the item list is read-heavy and barely changes — that's why the MySQL Pod pegs near its CPU limit under load while its logs show the exact same query repeating, pure wasted work a cache could have served instead.
`redis-service:6379` is already deployed and already wired into the backend's env — the fix isn't infrastructure, it's the read path's logic: apply cache-aside.
On `GET /items`, check Redis first for the `items_list` key; a hit returns immediately with `source: "cache"`, never touching MySQL.
A miss queries MySQL, builds the response, `SET`s it into Redis with a TTL (say 60s), and returns `source: "database"` for that one call only.

The TTL is a backstop, not the main correctness guarantee — that comes from invalidation: `POST /items` must `DEL` the `items_list` key the moment it writes, guaranteeing the very next `GET /items` misses and repopulates from MySQL instead of serving a stale list missing the item just created.
Verify the cache path by calling `GET /items` twice in a row and confirming the second response flips to `source: "cache"`.
Verify the load-reduction by replaying the same load and watching `kubectl top pod -l app=mysql` settle down while logs stop repeating the query on every call.
Verify invalidation by confirming a `POST /items` followed immediately by `GET /items` shows the new item on that very next read, never a stale cached list.
`Pending` means the scheduler could not fit the pod anywhere on the node, not that anything crashed.

The full stack (sharded MongoDB + PostgreSQL HA + Redis cluster, ≈22 pods) sums to well over 8GB of requested RAM, while the `kind` node only has 8GB total — so roughly half the pods simply have nowhere to schedule.
The fix is not a bigger machine, it is a lighter install: bring up only one representative chart instead of all three stacks.
Names a concrete lighter choice, e.g. PostgreSQL HA alone (~5 pods), rather than the full 22-pod stack.
Override resource-heavy defaults down through `values.yaml` (e.g. `replicaCount`, `persistence.size`) instead of trusting the chart's production-sized defaults.
Verify by `kubectl get pods`: previously `Pending` pods should now read `Running`.
Verify by `kubectl describe pod` on a previously `Pending` pod: it should no longer show an insufficient-resources event.
